opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated aspects of the whole o1 story. For a long time, the nice thing about LLMs was that they were essentially pay-per-token and the cost of a query was roughly proportional to the length of the answer. You asked something, it gave you an autocomplete, and you paid for that. With o1-style models, you're now paying for all these "reasoning tokens" that you don't even get to see, and the number of them is decided by the system, not by you. So the cost of a single query can vary wildly, and it's often much higher than people expect.

Once you start paying that kind of price, the question changes. It's no longer "is this LLM good enough?" but "is this the right tool for this problem at this price?" And the point we've been making in our work is that for a lot of problems, especially planning and scheduling kinds of problems, there are classical solvers that are guaranteed correct, run on a laptop, and cost essentially nothing per instance. If you're going to spend dollars per query on a reasoning model that still doesn't give you guarantees, you have to ask why you aren't just calling a planner, or using an LLM-Modulo setup where a cheaper LLM generates candidates and external verifiers check them.

So in our evaluations, when we looked at o1-preview on PlanBench, yes, it did significantly better than previous LLMs on Blocksworld and so on, which is to its credit. But the accuracy degrades as problems get longer, it still fails on obfuscated versions, and it's not cheap. Then you compare it to Fast Downward, which solves all of these correctly in a fraction of a second, and the cost-benefit picture looks very different.

I think the right way to think about it is that these reasoning models are moving us from a world where everything is one general-purpose autocomplete to a world where you have to think about cost, accuracy, and guarantees together. In other words, it's an engineering trade-off again. Sometimes the generality is worth paying for, especially when you don't have a formal model of the domain. But when you do have one, or can get one, it's hard to justify paying a lot for an approximate answer when an exact and cheap one exists. People will have to start making those choices consciously, rather than just saying "throw the biggest model at it."

r002.rationale: It does not claim that high costs have limited academic experimentation or evaluation.

r003.rationale: It discusses cost, accuracy, and guarantees, but does not describe computational complexity constraints reemerging after being overlooked during autoregressive generation.

r004.rationale: It frames reasoning cost as a tool-choice factor and compares general-purpose reasoning models, an LLM-plus-verifier setup, and specialized classical solvers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated aspects of the whole o1 story. Everybody got excited about the performance, but very few people looked at the cost column. And the cost column is where the real story is.

So here is the thing. For the last couple of years, we had this clean separation. LLMs were cheap and fast. You send a prompt, you get a completion, you pay for the tokens you see. The whole value proposition was: it's approximate, it's a vibe, but it's cheap. And then people, including me, were saying, look, if you want guarantees, you have to pair the LLM with a verifier, a planner, a solver. The LLM-Modulo approach, as we called it. The LLM generates, something sound checks.

Now what o1 does is it internalizes a kind of search, or at least something that looks like search, into inference time. And you pay for that. You pay for all the hidden "reasoning tokens" that you never even get to see. So suddenly the LLM is no longer the cheap approximate thing. It is an expensive thing, and the cost is not fixed. It depends on how hard the problem is, or really, how hard the model thinks the problem is, because you have no control over how long it deliberates.

And that completely changes the engineering calculus. Think about it. If I have a planning problem, a scheduling problem, a constraint satisfaction problem, I have had, for decades, very good solvers for these. They are complete, they are sound, they give you guarantees, and they run on a laptop for essentially zero marginal cost. Why would I pay a hundred times the per-token price to get a system that gives me no guarantee, and that I cannot even predict the cost of ahead of time? The moment you say the LLM is going to be expensive, you have to ask, expensive compared to what? And compared to a classical solver, it is not even close.

Where it does make sense is the messy, underspecified end. Problems where you cannot even write down the formal model, where the LLM's broad knowledge is the asset. There, maybe spending the extra inference compute is worth it. But I think people are going to be surprised at how narrow that band is once they actually do the accounting. For a large class of practical problems, the right design is still: cheap LLM for the fuzzy parts, external verifier or solver for the parts that need correctness. o1 doesn't eliminate that, it just moves the cost around, and frankly makes it harder to see.

The other thing I'd say is that the opacity is a problem in itself. OpenAI is hiding the reasoning traces, so you can't inspect them, you can't audit them, you can't tell whether the compute was well spent. You are paying for thinking you aren't allowed to see. From a systems design perspective, that's a strange thing to build on. So my short answer is: the cost of o1-style reasoning makes the case for hybrid, modular systems stronger, not weaker. It is just that now the LLM is one expensive component among several, rather than the free lunch people had been treating it as.

r001.rationale: The response says users pay for hidden reasoning tokens and cannot inspect the reasoning traces, but it does not say that the reported token quantity is something users must take on trust.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss academic experimentation or say that high cost has limited evaluation.

r003.rationale: It describes variable inference costs and compares o1 with classical solvers, but does not communicate that computational complexity constraints reemerge after being largely overlooked during autoregressive generation.

r004.rationale: It uses cost to argue for choosing among expensive LLM reasoning, hybrid LLM-verifier or solver designs, and specialized classical solvers.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes the question of when to reason much more important. If you spend a lot more computation on every query, then even an improvement in accuracy may not justify the cost. For a simple question, you might prefer a cheaper model. For a difficult problem where an error is expensive, spending more computation could be worthwhile.

But I would separate spending more time from having a guarantee that the answer is correct. A longer reasoning trace is not itself a verification procedure. If you can check the result with an external verifier, then additional computation can support a useful process: generate a candidate, check it, and try again if necessary.

So the choice is increasingly about the whole system. Where do you use a language model, where do you use a specialized solver, and how do you decide that you've spent enough? You want the additional computation to buy you something you can actually assess.

r004.rationale: It says system choice depends on where to use a language model versus a specialized solver, and on whether extra computation is worthwhile.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes the question of when to reason much more important. If you spend a lot more computation on every question, then you have to ask whether the improvement is worth that cost. For a simple question, probably it isn’t. For a difficult planning problem, it might be—especially if you can check whether the answer actually satisfies the constraints.

So I don’t see this as choosing one system that does everything. You want a system that can decide when a quick response is sufficient, when to spend more effort, and when to call an external solver or verifier. And spending more time generating an answer doesn’t, by itself, make that answer correct. The choice should depend on the task, the cost of computation, and the cost of being wrong.
